claim: The repeating subunit of chromatin, the nucleosome, includes two copies of each of the four core histones.
source: The repeating subunit of chromatin, the nucleosome, includes two copies of each of the four core histones, and several recent studies have reported that asymmetrically-modified nucleosomes occur at regulatory elements in vivo.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about nucleosome structure.

claim: Several recent studies have reported that asymmetrically-modified nucleosomes occur at regulatory elements in vivo.
source: The repeating subunit of chromatin, the nucleosome, includes two copies of each of the four core histones, and several recent studies have reported that asymmetrically-modified nucleosomes occur at regulatory elements in vivo.
evidence: This claim references recent studies, indicating citation-based support.

claim: H3X and H3Y are an obligate pair of H3 heterodimers that have been extensively validated genetically and biochemically.
source: To probe the mechanisms by which histone modifications are read out, we designed an obligate pair of H3 heterodimers, termed H3X and H3Y, which we extensively validated genetically and biochemically.
evidence: The manuscript presents genetic and biochemical validation data for H3X and H3Y throughout the Results section.

claim: A single methylated H3K36 per nucleosome is sufficient to silence cryptic transcription in vivo.
source: Comparing the effects of asymmetric histone tail point mutants with those of symmetric double mutants revealed that a single methylated H3K36 per nucleosome was sufficient to silence cryptic transcription in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing asymmetric and symmetric mutants presented in the manuscript.

claim: The H3X/H3Y system can be used for analysis of histone modification crosstalk using mass spectrometry.
source: We also demonstrate the utility of this system for analysis of histone modification crosstalk, using mass spectrometry to separately identify modifications on each H3 molecule within asymmetric nucleosomes.
evidence: The manuscript presents mass spectrometry data demonstrating this utility.

claim: The ability to generate asymmetric nucleosomes in vivo and in vitro provides a tool to probe mechanisms by which H3 tails are read out by effector proteins.
source: The ability to generate asymmetric nucleosomes in vivo and in vitro provides a powerful and generalizable tool to probe the mechanisms by which H3 tails are read out by effector proteins in the cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental work presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nucleosomes generally impede the access of proteins to the underlying DNA.
source: Packaging of eukaryotic genomes into chromatin has widespread consequences for genomic function, as nucleosomes generally impede the access of proteins to the underlying DNA (Hughes and Rando, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hughes and Rando, 2014.

claim: Histone proteins are subject to a huge variety of covalent modifications.
source: In addition, the histone proteins are subject to a huge variety of covalent modifications, which affect genomic function in ways ranging from direct alterations in the biophysical nature of the chromatin fiber to recruitment or activation of various regulatory proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of chromatin biology.

claim: Histone modifications affect genomic function through direct alterations in the biophysical nature of the chromatin fiber and through recruitment or activation of regulatory proteins.
source: In addition, the histone proteins are subject to a huge variety of covalent modifications, which affect genomic function in ways ranging from direct alterations in the biophysical nature of the chromatin fiber to recruitment or activation of various regulatory proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge in chromatin biology.

claim: The histone octamer is comprised of two copies of each of the four histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4.
source: The histone octamer is comprised of two copies of each of the four histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4, organized with two H2A/H2B dimers associated with a central core tetramer of histone H3 and H4 (Kornberg and Lorch, 1999).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citation to Kornberg and Lorch, 1999.

claim: The histone octamer is organized with two H2A/H2B dimers associated with a central core tetramer of histone H3 and H4.
source: The histone octamer is comprised of two copies of each of the four histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4, organized with two H2A/H2B dimers associated with a central core tetramer of histone H3 and H4 (Kornberg and Lorch, 1999).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citation to Kornberg and Lorch, 1999.

claim: Chromatin function may be regulated at the level of histone modification symmetry.
source: The symmetry inherent to the histone octamer has long been appreciated, and it has been suggested that chromatin function may be regulated at the level of histone modification symmetry – that K4me3/K4me0 and K4me3/K4me3 nucleosomes might serve distinct functions in vivo, for example.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that has been suggested in the field.

claim: Immunopurification and mass spectrometry of nucleosomes marked with H3K27me3 in mammals revealed a mixture of symmetrically-modified nucleosomes and asymmetric nucleosomes modified on only one H3 tail.
source: In mammals, immunopurification and mass spectrometry of nucleosomes marked with H3K27me3 revealed a mixture of symmetrically-modified nucleosomes as well as asymmetric nucleosomes modified on only one H3 tail (Voigt et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Voigt et al., 2012.

claim: The vast majority of H3K4me3/K27me3-marked 'bivalent' nucleosomes are asymmetrically modified, with each H3 tail bearing one of the two methylation marks.
source: More recent single molecule studies of H3K4me3/K27me3-marked 'bivalent' nucleosomes reveal that the vast majority of these nucleosomes are asymmetrically modified, with each H3 tail bearing one of the two methylation marks, rather than both marks co-occurring on the same H3 molecule (Shema et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shema et al., 2016.

claim: In budding yeast, ChIP-Exo and chemical mapping studies identified a subset of nucleosomes that exhibit asymmetric contacts with the underlying genomic DNA.
source: In budding yeast, ChIP-Exo and chemical mapping studies identified a subset of nucleosomes that exhibit asymmetric contacts with the underlying genomic DNA (Rhee et al., 2014; Ramachandran et al., 2015), suggested to reflect histone octamers associated with an asymmetrically-localized DNA bulge.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rhee et al., 2014 and Ramachandran et al., 2015.

claim: Asymmetric nucleosome contacts with DNA are suggested to reflect histone octamers associated with an asymmetrically-localized DNA bulge.
source: In budding yeast, ChIP-Exo and chemical mapping studies identified a subset of nucleosomes that exhibit asymmetric contacts with the underlying genomic DNA (Rhee et al., 2014; Ramachandran et al., 2015), suggested to reflect histone octamers associated with an asymmetrically-localized DNA bulge.
evidence: This is a suggested interpretation of the data from the cited studies.

claim: The histone acetyltransferase Gcn5 exhibits cooperative binding to two histone tails.
source: For instance, Li et al assembled and purified asymmetric nucleosomes lacking a single H3 tail in vitro, subsequently showing that the histone acetyltransferase Gcn5 exhibited cooperative binding to two histone tails (Li and Shogren-Knaak, 2008; Li and Shogren-Knaak, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li and Shogren-Knaak, 2008 and 2009.

claim: Asymmetrically H3K4-methylated nucleosomes are efficiently methylated at K27 by the PRC2 complex, like unmodified nucleosomes.
source: Conversely, asymmetrically H3K4-methylated nucleosomes were, like unmodified nucleosomes, efficiently methylated at K27 by the PRC2 complex, whereas this methylation was inhibited by the presence of symmetric H3K4me3 marks (Voigt et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Voigt et al., 2012.

claim: K27 methylation by PRC2 is inhibited by the presence of symmetric H3K4me3 marks.
source: Conversely, asymmetrically H3K4-methylated nucleosomes were, like unmodified nucleosomes, efficiently methylated at K27 by the PRC2 complex, whereas this methylation was inhibited by the presence of symmetric H3K4me3 marks (Voigt et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Voigt et al., 2012.

claim: The inherent symmetry of the natural H3-H3 interface has made in vivo tests of nucleosome symmetry hypotheses impossible until now.
source: Although these in vitro studies generate hypotheses for how chromatin effectors might be affected by nucleosome symmetry in the cell, the inherent symmetry of the natural H3-H3 interface has made in vivo tests of these hypotheses impossible until now.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of previous approaches.

claim: H3X and H3Y form heterodimers in vivo but cannot homodimerize.
source: Using rational design, followed by in vivo optimization and selection, we developed a pair of H3 proteins – H3X and H3Y – that form heterodimers in vivo, yet cannot homodimerize.
evidence: This is supported by genetic and biochemical validation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The vast majority of histone octamers in yeast cells expressing H3X and H3Y contain a heterodimeric H3X/H3Y at their core.
source: We validated this system genetically and biochemically in budding yeast, confirming that the vast majority of histone octamers in the cell contain a heterodimeric H3X/H3Y at their core.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical data showing ~97% heterodimer formation.

claim: The engineered H3X/H3Y specificities are recapitulated in vitro during biochemical reconstitution of histone octamers with recombinant subunits.
source: Furthermore, we confirm that the engineered specificities are recapitulated in vitro during biochemical reconstitution of histone octamers with recombinant subunits.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro reconstitution data presented in Figure 3.

claim: A single copy of H3K36 is sufficient for stress resistance in vivo.
source: We then used this system to probe several mechanistic aspects of nucleosome function in vivo, finding that a single copy of H3K36 is sufficient for stress resistance, and to silence cryptic transcription, in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Disruption of H3S10 affects H3K9 acetylation only on the same tail.
source: In addition, we show that disruption of H3S10 affects H3K9 acetylation only on the same tail, demonstrating the utility of this approach for interrogating histone 'crosstalk'.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry and Western blot data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The histone octamer is built on a central core tetramer of histone H3 and H4, assembled around a central H3-H3 homodimeric interface.
source: The histone octamer is built on a central core tetramer of histone H3 and H4, assembled around a central H3-H3 homodimeric interface (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citation to Luger et al., 1997.

claim: Six sets of H3 mutants were designed that are predicted to have much higher affinity with a paired mutant protein than with wild-type H3.
source: We initially used protein design to develop six sets of H3 mutants that are predicted to have much higher affinity with a paired mutant protein than with wild-type H3.
evidence: This describes the computational design approach used.

claim: The engineered H3 variants have 'bumps and holes' that are predicted to reduce the potential for homodimerization.
source: Each engineered variant has 'bumps and holes' that are also predicted to reduce the potential for homodimerization.
evidence: This describes the design strategy used for the H3 variants.

claim: The design focused on the hydrophobic cluster formed by amino acids L109, A110, L126, and L130 in the nucleosome structure.
source: We focused our efforts on the hydrophobic cluster formed by amino acids L109, A110, L126, and L130 (Figure 1B) in the nucleosome structure (pdb 1KX3).
evidence: This describes the specific residues targeted in the design.

claim: Yeast carrying H3Y alone exhibited no growth even after 21 days of culture.
source: However, although yeast carrying H3Y alone exhibited no growth even after 21 days of culture (Figure 1C and not shown), H3X-only strains did grow even in the absence of H3Y, albeit poorly – colonies were only observed after nine or more days of growth of these strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), in contrast to the abundant colonies observed for H3X/H3Y strains after just two or three days.
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Initial H3X-only strains grew poorly in the absence of H3Y, with colonies only observed after nine or more days.
source: However, although yeast carrying H3Y alone exhibited no growth even after 21 days of culture (Figure 1C and not shown), H3X-only strains did grow even in the absence of H3Y, albeit poorly – colonies were only observed after nine or more days of growth of these strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), in contrast to the abundant colonies observed for H3X/H3Y strains after just two or three days.
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H3X/H3Y strains showed abundant colonies after two or three days of growth.
source: However, although yeast carrying H3Y alone exhibited no growth even after 21 days of culture (Figure 1C and not shown), H3X-only strains did grow even in the absence of H3Y, albeit poorly – colonies were only observed after nine or more days of growth of these strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), in contrast to the abundant colonies observed for H3X/H3Y strains after just two or three days.
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data.

claim: Four final versions of H3X (126A, 130A, 130T, and 130Q) conferred robust growth in the presence of H3Y but were completely inviable in its absence.
source: In this manner, we identified four final versions of H3X (named 126A, 130A, 130T, and 130Q for the additional substitutions on the original H3X backbone) that reproducibly conferred robust growth in the presence of H3Y but were completely inviable in its absence (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: L126A and L130A mutations cause lethality when present on symmetric H3 molecules.
source: Consistent with our observation that these residues are sensitive points for H3/H3 dimeric interactions, L126A and L130A mutations cause lethality when present on symmetric H3 molecules (Dai et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dai et al., 2008.

claim: The DMS crosslinking efficiency of the X-Y heterodimeric pairs was nearly identical to that observed in cells expressing tagged H3 variants with a wild-type, homodimeric interface.
source: The DMS crosslinking efficiency of the X-Y heterodimeric pairs was nearly identical to that observed in cells expressing tagged H3 variants with a wild-type, homodimeric interface (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by crosslinking data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Barely detectable levels of V5-H3X were observed in the bound 31kD species, indicating minimal H3X-H3X homodimerization.
source: In contrast, barely detectable levels of V5-H3X – which would result from H3X-H3X homodimerization – were observed in the bound 31kD species (Figure 2B, quantitated in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B and quantitation in Figure 2C.

claim: Barely detectable H3Y homodimerization was observed in reciprocal experiments.
source: In a reciprocal experiment, we assayed H3Y homodimerization, again finding efficient heterodimerization in vivo along with barely detectable H3Y homodimerization (Figure 2D–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Gel filtration of in vitro assembled octamers revealed robust assembly of histone octamers using wild-type H3 or the H3X/H3Y heterodimer pair.
source: Gel filtration of in vitro assembled octamers revealed robust assembly of histone octamers assembled using wild-type H3, or assembled around the H3X/H3Y heterodimer pair.
evidence: This is supported by gel filtration data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Attempts to refold histone octamers using H3X only or H3Y only resulted in high molecular weight aggregates with no functional histone octamer.
source: In contrast, attempts to refold histone octamers using H3X only or H3Y only resulted in high molecular weight aggregates with no functional histone octamer (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by gel filtration data shown in Figure 3.

claim: H3X/H3Y-based octamers were readily reconstituted into nucleosomes when assembled with DNA.
source: Moreover, H3X/H3Y-based octamers were readily reconstituted into nucleosomes when assembled with DNA, whereas the material obtained from H3X alone or H3Y alone did not assemble into nucleosomes.
evidence: This is supported by nucleosome reconstitution data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Material obtained from H3X alone or H3Y alone did not assemble into nucleosomes.
source: Moreover, H3X/H3Y-based octamers were readily reconstituted into nucleosomes when assembled with DNA, whereas the material obtained from H3X alone or H3Y alone did not assemble into nucleosomes.
evidence: This is supported by nucleosome reconstitution data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The great majority (average of ~97%) of nucleosomes in vivo are heterodimeric H3X/H3Y.
source: Taken together, our genetic and biochemical analyses validate our designed obligate heterodimers, indicating that the great majority (average of ~97% as measured in Figure 2C,F) if not all of the nucleosomes in vivo are indeed heterodimeric.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative biochemical data shown in Figure 2C and 2F.

claim: Strains expressing the heterodimeric X/Y H3s exhibit reduced growth in YPD with doubling times of ~240 min at 30°C compared to ~140 min for the parent strain.
source: Importantly, although strains expressing the heterodimeric X/Y H3s exhibit reduced growth in YPD (doubling times of ~240 min at 30°C compared to ~140 min for the parent strain, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and a modest temperature-sensitive phenotype (robust growth at 34 C but failure to grow at 37 C – see below), any effects of the mutant X/Y interface on chromatin regulation and cellular function are internally controlled for in all studies by comparing all yeast carrying single or double histone mutations to the 'pseudo-wild type' strain (H3Xwt/H3Ywt).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Strains expressing the heterodimeric X/Y H3s exhibit a modest temperature-sensitive phenotype with robust growth at 34°C but failure to grow at 37°C.
source: Importantly, although strains expressing the heterodimeric X/Y H3s exhibit reduced growth in YPD (doubling times of ~240 min at 30°C compared to ~140 min for the parent strain, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and a modest temperature-sensitive phenotype (robust growth at 34 C but failure to grow at 37 C – see below), any effects of the mutant X/Y interface on chromatin regulation and cellular function are internally controlled for in all studies by comparing all yeast carrying single or double histone mutations to the 'pseudo-wild type' strain (H3Xwt/H3Ywt).
evidence: This is supported by temperature sensitivity assays.

claim: Growth rates for strains carrying a single mutation on H3X were generally well-correlated with those for H3Y mutants.
source: As expected, growth rates for strains carrying a single mutation on H3X were generally well-correlated with those for H3Y mutants, although a small subset of mutations exhibited different behavior on different H3 backbones (see, eg, H3K37Q in 0.8M KCl).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: A small subset of mutations exhibited different behavior on different H3 backbones.
source: As expected, growth rates for strains carrying a single mutation on H3X were generally well-correlated with those for H3Y mutants, although a small subset of mutations exhibited different behavior on different H3 backbones (see, eg, H3K37Q in 0.8M KCl).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 4A-B, specifically the H3K37Q example.

claim: Yeast carrying double H3K14R, H3K14Q, or H3K36Q mutations exhibited significantly diminished growth, particularly in high salt.
source: In contrast, we noted significantly diminished growth, particularly in high salt, for yeast carrying double H3K14R, H3K14Q, or H3K36Q mutations (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For H3K14R, single mutants exhibited a partial growth defect that was exacerbated in the double mutant.
source: Interestingly, the behaviors of the corresponding asymmetric single mutants were distinct: for H3K14R, single mutants already exhibited a partial growth defect that was exacerbated in the double mutant, while for H3K36Q the single mutant strains had no measurable deficit compared to the pseudo-wild type.
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 4.

claim: For H3K36Q, single mutant strains had no measurable deficit compared to the pseudo-wild type.
source: Interestingly, the behaviors of the corresponding asymmetric single mutants were distinct: for H3K14R, single mutants already exhibited a partial growth defect that was exacerbated in the double mutant, while for H3K36Q the single mutant strains had no measurable deficit compared to the pseudo-wild type.
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Yeast lacking H3K36 methylation are hypersensitive to DNA damaging agents.
source: Consistent with prior studies demonstrating that yeast lacking H3K36 methylation are hypersensitive to DNA damaging agents (Jha and Strahl, 2014), we find that the K36Q double mutants – but neither of the single K36Q mutants – displayed increased sensitivity to both the DNA alkylating agent methyl methanesulfonate (MMS) and the strand break-inducing agent phleomycin (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jha and Strahl, 2014.

claim: K36Q double mutants displayed increased sensitivity to both MMS and phleomycin, but neither of the single K36Q mutants did.
source: Consistent with prior studies demonstrating that yeast lacking H3K36 methylation are hypersensitive to DNA damaging agents (Jha and Strahl, 2014), we find that the K36Q double mutants – but neither of the single K36Q mutants – displayed increased sensitivity to both the DNA alkylating agent methyl methanesulfonate (MMS) and the strand break-inducing agent phleomycin (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by DNA damage sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Symmetric double K36Q mutants exhibited reduced growth at 34°C, while asymmetric mutants exhibited similar or only slightly reduced growth compared to the pseudo-wild type.
source: Moreover, these mutants were also temperature-sensitive, as symmetric double mutants exhibited reduced growth at 34 C, while the asymmetric mutants exhibited similar or only slightly reduced growth compared to the pseudo-wild type under these conditions (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by temperature sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: K36Q mutations confer sensitivity to osmotic, temperature and DNA damage stresses only when symmetrically present on nucleosomes.
source: We conclude that K36Q mutations confer sensitivity to osmotic, temperature and DNA damage stresses, but only when symmetrically present on nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the growth and stress sensitivity data presented.

claim: H3K36 is methylated by Set2.
source: H3K36 is methylated by Set2 (Strahl et al., 2002), with the resulting modified residues serving to activate the RPD3S histone deacetylase complex via binding of the Eaf3 chromodomain-containing subunit (Carrozza et al., 2005; Keogh et al., 2005; Joshi and Struhl, 2005; Govind et al., 2010; Drouin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Strahl et al., 2002.

claim: H3K36 methylation activates the RPD3S histone deacetylase complex via binding of the Eaf3 chromodomain-containing subunit.
source: H3K36 is methylated by Set2 (Strahl et al., 2002), with the resulting modified residues serving to activate the RPD3S histone deacetylase complex via binding of the Eaf3 chromodomain-containing subunit (Carrozza et al., 2005; Keogh et al., 2005; Joshi and Struhl, 2005; Govind et al., 2010; Drouin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The major biological role served by H3K36 methylation is silencing of cryptic internal promoters via activation of the RPD3S complex.
source: As the major biological role served by H3K36 methylation is silencing of cryptic internal promoters via activation of the RPD3S complex (Carrozza et al., 2005), and given that RPD3S can bind to nucleosomes with a single H3K36me3 modification (Huh et al., 2012), we sought to test whether a single methylated H3K36 per nucleosome would be sufficient to support robust silencing of such cryptic transcripts in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Carrozza et al., 2005.

claim: RPD3S can bind to nucleosomes with a single H3K36me3 modification.
source: As the major biological role served by H3K36 methylation is silencing of cryptic internal promoters via activation of the RPD3S complex (Carrozza et al., 2005), and given that RPD3S can bind to nucleosomes with a single H3K36me3 modification (Huh et al., 2012), we sought to test whether a single methylated H3K36 per nucleosome would be sufficient to support robust silencing of such cryptic transcripts in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Huh et al., 2012.

claim: P38V mutations eliminate the possibility of proline isomerization and block trimethylation but not dimethylation of the nearby K36 residue.
source: The P38V mutants enable di- and tri-methylation of H3K36 to be distinguished – the wild-type proline residue at this position undergoes regulated isomerization, and P38V mutations that eliminate the possibility of proline isomerization block trimethylation (Nelson et al., 2006) but not dimethylation (Youdell et al., 2008) of the nearby K36 residue, a finding that we confirm here (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nelson et al., 2006 and Youdell et al., 2008, and confirmed by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cells expressing only H3P38V display none of the cryptic transcription phenotypes observed in set2, eaf3, or H3K36Q mutants.
source: Importantly, cells expressing only H3P38V display none of the cryptic transcription phenotypes observed in set2, eaf3, or H3K36Q mutants ([Youdell et al., 2008] and see below), indicating that H3K36me2 is sufficient for the proper activation of the Rpd3S complex with regards to repression of cryptic transcription.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Youdell et al., 2008 and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: H3K36me2 is sufficient for the proper activation of the Rpd3S complex with regards to repression of cryptic transcription.
source: Importantly, cells expressing only H3P38V display none of the cryptic transcription phenotypes observed in set2, eaf3, or H3K36Q mutants ([Youdell et al., 2008] and see below), indicating that H3K36me2 is sufficient for the proper activation of the Rpd3S complex with regards to repression of cryptic transcription.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the P38V mutant phenotype data.

claim: Double P38V mutations did not cause the temperature sensitivity observed in K36Q mutant cells.
source: Consistent with this, we find that double P38V mutations, on either a wild-type H3 backbone or in the context of the XY system, did not cause the temperature sensitivity observed in K36Q mutant cells (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by temperature sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: K36Q/P38V trans strains have one H3 tail that lacks K36 methylation entirely and one tail with a dimethylated K36 residue.
source: Consistent with previous analyses of the effects of P38V (Nelson et al., 2006; Youdell et al., 2008), immunoblotting confirms that these strains have one H3 tail (K36Q) that lacks K36 methylation entirely, and one tail (P38V) with a dimethylated K36 residue (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Neither K36Q/P38V trans strain is sensitive to growth at 34°C or DNA damaging agents.
source: Notably, neither of these K36Q/P38V trans strains are sensitive to growth at 34C (Figure 4F) or DNA damaging agents (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figures 4C and 4F.

claim: A single K36me2 is sufficient to promote stress tolerance in budding yeast.
source: These data indicate that a single K36me2 is sufficient to promote stress tolerance in budding yeast.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the K36Q/P38V trans strain phenotype data.

claim: Eaf3Δ mutants show increased cryptic transcription at STE11.
source: First, we confirmed the expected increase in cryptic transcription in eaf3Δ mutants, and in yeast carrying symmetric H3K36Q mutations on the wild-type H3 backbone (Figure 5A–B, lanes 1–4, 10).
evidence: This is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Yeast carrying symmetric H3K36Q mutations on the wild-type H3 backbone show increased cryptic transcription at STE11.
source: First, we confirmed the expected increase in cryptic transcription in eaf3Δ mutants, and in yeast carrying symmetric H3K36Q mutations on the wild-type H3 backbone (Figure 5A–B, lanes 1–4, 10).
evidence: This is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: H3P38V mutants did not cause significantly increased cryptic transcription at STE11.
source: In addition, we confirm that H3K36me2 was sufficient to silence the STE11 cryptic promoter, as H3P38V mutants (which lack H3K36me3 but exhibit normal H3K36me2 levels) did not cause significantly increased cryptic transcription (lane 5).
evidence: This is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 5A-B, lane 5.

claim: Pseudo-wildtype H3X/Y cells and cells with a single K36Q mutated tail display similar, low levels of cryptic transcripts at STE11.
source: Consistent with the growth phenotypes observed in Figure 4, we find that the pseudo-wildtype H3X/Y cells and the cells with a single K36Q mutated tail display similar, low levels of cryptic transcripts (lanes 6–8).
evidence: This is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 5A-B, lanes 6-8.

claim: Cells with two K36Q mutated tails display greatly elevated cryptic transcript levels at STE11.
source: In contrast, the cells with two K36Q mutated tails display greatly elevated cryptic transcript levels (lane 9).
evidence: This is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 5A-B, lane 9.

claim: Neither single nor double P38V mutant tails affected cryptic transcription at STE11.
source: As expected, neither single nor double P38V mutant tails affected cryptic transcription in our strain background (lanes 14–16).
evidence: This is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 5A-B, lanes 14-16.

claim: P38V/K36Q trans strains displayed modest derepression of cryptic transcription at STE11, more similar to single K36Q mutants than K36Q double mutants.
source: Finally, P38V/K36Q trans strains (lanes 17–18) displayed modest derepression of cryptic transcription, more similar to that observed in single K36Q mutant cells (lanes 7–8) than the high level observed in K36Q double mutants (lane 9).
evidence: This is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 5A-B, lanes 17-18.

claim: Derepression of cryptic transcription at FLO8 was observed specifically in the K36Q double mutant, but not in either K36Q single mutant.
source: We confirmed the generality of these findings using another well-studied model for cryptic transcription, the FLO8 locus (Kaplan et al., 2003), where derepression of cryptic transcription was again observed specifically in the K36Q double mutant, but not in either K36Q single mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A single K36-di-methylated H3 tail per nucleosome is sufficient to restrain cryptic transcription in vivo.
source: We conclude that a single K36-di-methylated H3 tail per nucleosome is sufficient to restrain cryptic transcription in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cryptic transcription data for K36Q and P38V mutants.

claim: Biotin-tagged H3 molecules were purified with >93% purity away from the untagged H3 molecule from each nucleosome.
source: Analysis of peptides derived from the engineered H3X/H3Y interface confirmed our ability to efficiently purify the biotin-tagged H3 molecule away from the untagged H3 molecule from each nucleosome, with >93% purity observed for informative peptides analyzed (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The fraction of H3 molecules acetylated at K9 was lower in yeast strains carrying H3S10A symmetrically.
source: We found that the fraction of H3 molecules acetylated at K9 was lower in yeast strains carrying H3S10A symmetrically, either on a wild-type histone backbone or in the H3X/H3Y system.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry and Western blot data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: H3K9 acetylation levels were significantly decreased on the same histone tail carrying the S10A mutation, but were not affected by the presence of H3S10A in trans.
source: Turning next to analysis of asymmetric mutant nucleosomes, mass spectrometric analyses showed that H3K9 acetylation levels were significantly decreased on the same histone tail carrying the S10A mutation, but were not affected by the presence of H3S10A in trans (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Western blotting confirmed that H3S10A affects adjacent H3K9 acetylation on the same tail, but has no effect on modification of a paired wild-type H3 tail.
source: Western blotting for H3K9ac in yeast strains where an epitope tag allows H3X and H3Y isoforms to be separated by gel electrophoresis confirmed our mass spec-based analysis of histone acetylation, with H3S10A affecting adjacent H3K9 acetylation on the same tail, but having no effect on modification of a paired wild-type H3 tail (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C-F.

claim: Immunopurification and mass spectrometry of nucleosomes marked with H3K27me3 revealed asymmetric nucleosomes in mammals.
source: In mammals, immunopurification and mass spectrometry of nucleosomes marked with H3K27me3 revealed a mixture of symmetrically-modified nucleosomes as well as asymmetric nucleosomes modified on only one H3 tail (Voigt et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Voigt et al., 2012.

claim: Single molecule studies revealed that the vast majority of H3K4me3/K27me3-marked 'bivalent' nucleosomes are asymmetrically modified.
source: More recent single molecule studies of H3K4me3/K27me3-marked 'bivalent' nucleosomes reveal that the vast majority of these nucleosomes are asymmetrically modified, with each H3 tail bearing one of the two methylation marks, rather than both marks co-occurring on the same H3 molecule (Shema et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shema et al., 2016.

claim: Asymmetrically H3K4-methylated nucleosomes were efficiently methylated at K27 by the PRC2 complex.
source: Conversely, asymmetrically H3K4-methylated nucleosomes were, like unmodified nucleosomes, efficiently methylated at K27 by the PRC2 complex, whereas this methylation was inhibited by the presence of symmetric H3K4me3 marks (Voigt et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Voigt et al., 2012.

claim: RPD3S appears to be particularly well-suited to carrying out its regulatory functions even on chromatin that is less than fully methylated at H3K36.
source: Notably, the RPD3S complex appears to be particularly well-suited to carrying out its regulatory functions even on chromatin that is less than fully methylated at H3K36.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and in vitro binding studies.

claim: RPD3S binds with higher affinity to dinucleosomes than monosomes.
source: Further, although RPD3S binds with higher affinity to dinucleosomes than monosomes, it binds with high affinity to templates with a dimethylated nucleosome adjacent to a fully unmethylated one.
evidence: This is based on in vitro binding studies referenced in the discussion.

claim: RPD3S binds with high affinity to templates with a dimethylated nucleosome adjacent to a fully unmethylated one.
source: Further, although RPD3S binds with higher affinity to dinucleosomes than monosomes, it binds with high affinity to templates with a dimethylated nucleosome adjacent to a fully unmethylated one.
evidence: This is based on in vitro binding studies referenced in the discussion.

claim: The methyl-K36/RPD3S system would be buffered against transient reductions in H3K36me2-3 density during DNA repair or replication-mediated loss of modified histones.
source: These data suggest that the methyl-K36/RPD3S system would be buffered against transient reductions in H3K36me2-3 density, for example during DNA repair or replication-mediated loss of modified histones.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the binding properties of RPD3S.

claim: The enzyme RPD3S can function effectively in vivo even if it can only engage a single H3K36me2 or me3 per nucleosome.
source: Our data extend these observations to indicate that the enzyme can function effectively in vivo even if it can only engage a single H3K36me2 or me3 per nucleosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on asymmetric K36 methylation.

claim: S10 phosphorylation stimulates H3 tail acetylation by Gcn5 only in cis.
source: This is consistent with a recent in vitro study demonstrating that S10 phosphorylation stimulates H3 tail acetylation by Gcn5 only in cis (Liokatis et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liokatis et al., 2016.

claim: The H3X/Y system should function appropriately in other species beyond budding yeast.
source: Although such studies are demonstrated here using the budding yeast system, the H3-H3 interface is generally highly conserved throughout evolution, and we expect that this system should function appropriately in other species – indeed, the biochemical reconstitution of asymmetric nucleosomes described in Figure 3 is carried out using human histone sequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation and demonstration with human histones.

claim: The biochemical reconstitution of asymmetric nucleosomes in Figure 3 is carried out using human histone sequences.
source: Although such studies are demonstrated here using the budding yeast system, the H3-H3 interface is generally highly conserved throughout evolution, and we expect that this system should function appropriately in other species – indeed, the biochemical reconstitution of asymmetric nucleosomes described in Figure 3 is carried out using human histone sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: The H3-H3 interface is generally highly conserved throughout evolution.
source: Although such studies are demonstrated here using the budding yeast system, the H3-H3 interface is generally highly conserved throughout evolution, and we expect that this system should function appropriately in other species – indeed, the biochemical reconstitution of asymmetric nucleosomes described in Figure 3 is carried out using human histone sequences.
evidence: This is established knowledge about histone sequence conservation.

claim: A Drosophila model has been developed in which the histone genes have been relocated to an artificial locus.
source: Although canonical histone genes are often encoded in many copies in large multi-gene genomic clusters and are therefore inconvenient for genetic studies, a Drosophila model has been developed in which the histone genes have been relocated to an artificial locus (McKay et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McKay et al., 2015.
